newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Defence claims alibi for Bosnian Serb in the dock.
newsitem.headline: Defence claims alibi for Bosnian Serb in the dock.

text.p: Defence lawyers for a Bosnian Serb accused of killing, torturing and raping Moslems at nearby concentration camps in the summer of 1992, claimed on Wednesday he was manning a checkpoint in northwest Bosnia at the time.
Miroslav Brdar, a Serb reserve policeman, told the U.N. tribunal for former Yugoslavia he and defendant Dusan Tadic manned the Orlovci checkpoint in northwest Bosnia in June and July 1992.
The prosecution alleges that during this period, Tadic, 41, entered prison camps at Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje to indulge in an orgy of torture, beatings and sexual assaults.

Defence lawyer Steven Kay presented the U.N. court with a copy of Tadic's rota for the Orlovci checkpoint from June 16 to August 1. Brdar confirmed that they were part of records held at Prijedor police station, drawn up by the station commander.
The rota detailed Tadic's shifts at the checkpoint, located six kilometres from Prijedor and around four kilometres from Omarska. They varied from six hour day shifts to 12 hour nights.
Brdar, a metal worker by trade, said it was impossible for those detailed to man checkpoints to go anywhere in the surrounding area without permission.
"You had to be on call when you were off-duty...No-one could go anywhere without permission," he said, adding that the posts were subject to surprise checks up to three times a day.
Asked whether it was possible for anyone manning the checkpoint to be absent for a significant amount of time, Brdar replied: "Something like that could not happen given the circumstances."
Tadic's defence has been beset by problems.

Difficulties in physically getting witnesses from Bosnia to The Hague courtroom, combined with some refusing to testify at the last minute for fear of their safety, have forced two delays in the proceedings in the last three weeks.
The trial, which began on May 7, is expected to continue into November, with a verdict forecast by next March.

The tribunal, the first international body to deal with war crimes since the Nuremburg and Tokyo trials after World War Two, has indicted over 70 Serbs, Croats and Moslems. It holds seven suspects in its Hague cells.
